articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County faces $12 million shortfall as tourism tax revenue drops
articles.dek: Commission meets Tuesday to consider cuts to road maintenance, library hours, and beach services ahead of fiscal year deadline.
brief: Escambia County projects a $12 million budget gap for fiscal year 2027, driven by a 14% decline in tourist development tax collections
County Administrator Wes Moreno has proposed reducing library hours, delaying road resurfacing projects, and cutting seasonal beach lifeguard positions
The Board of County Commissioners will hold a special budget session Tuesday at 9 a.m. to vote on preliminary cuts before the June 15 deadline
articles.body:
The projector in the Escambia County commission chamber displayed a single red number Tuesday morning: negative $12,247,000. County Administrator Wes Moreno let it sit there for a moment before speaking.

"That's our gap," Moreno told commissioners during a budget workshop. "And we have five weeks to close it."

Escambia County is staring down its largest budget shortfall since the pandemic years, driven primarily by a steep decline in tourist development tax revenue that funds beach services, marketing, and a portion of debt service on the county's sports complex. The TDT—a 5% tax on short-term lodging—brought in $18.3 million in fiscal year 2025. Current projections show collections dropping to $15.7 million for the fiscal year ending September 30, a 14% decline.

The shortfall compounds problems in the general fund, where property tax revenue grew slower than anticipated while costs for employee health insurance and liability coverage climbed faster than budgeted.

What's on the cutting board

Moreno presented commissioners with three tiers of potential cuts, ranging from $8 million to $14 million. The mid-range option, which staff recommended as a starting point, includes:

  • Reducing hours at five of the county's seven library branches from six days to four days per week, saving approximately $1.2 million
  • Delaying $4.3 million in scheduled road resurfacing projects in Districts 3 and 5
  • Eliminating 12 seasonal beach lifeguard positions at Perdido Key and Fort Pickens areas, saving $680,000
  • Freezing 23 vacant positions across multiple departments
  • Reducing the county's contribution to the Pensacola Bay Area Convention and Visitors Bureau by $1.8 million

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose District 1 includes Perdido Key, pushed back on the lifeguard cuts during Tuesday's workshop.

"We're talking about public safety at beaches that see a million visitors a year," Bergosh said. "I need to see other options before I can vote for that."

Commissioner Lumon May raised concerns about the road delays affecting his District 3, which includes some of the county's oldest infrastructure in the Brownsville and Tanyard neighborhoods.

"These roads were already on a five-year wait," May said. "Now we're telling folks seven years? Eight?"

Tourism's downward trend

The TDT decline reflects broader softening in Pensacola Beach tourism that began in late 2025. Hotel occupancy rates on Pensacola Beach averaged 61% for the first quarter of 2026, down from 72% during the same period last year, according to data from the Santa Rosa Island Authority.

Multiple factors appear to be contributing. Airfare to Pensacola International Airport rose 18% year-over-year according to Bureau of Transportation Statistics data. Gas prices, while lower than their 2022 peak, remain elevated compared to pre-pandemic levels. And competition from other Gulf destinations has intensified—Panama City Beach and Orange Beach both launched aggressive marketing campaigns targeting the same Southeastern drive markets.

"We're not seeing the weekend warriors like we used to," said Dana Jones, general manager of the Holiday Inn Resort on Pensacola Beach. "The four-night stays are down. The day-trippers from Mobile and Montgomery aren't coming like they did."

Jones said her property's April occupancy ran 15 percentage points below the same month in 2024.

The Visit Pensacola tourism bureau, which receives a dedicated share of TDT revenue, has already trimmed its advertising budget by $600,000 this year. The additional $1.8 million cut proposed by the county would force the organization to reduce staff and potentially cancel its fall sports tournament marketing program, according to bureau president Darien Schaefer.

"Sports tourism has been our growth engine," Schaefer said. "Pulling back now could hurt us for years."

The path forward

The Board of County Commissioners will meet in special session Tuesday, May 13, at 9 a.m. to vote on preliminary budget reductions. Florida law requires counties to submit tentative budgets to the state by June 15, with final budgets adopted in September after two public hearings.

Commission Chair Steven Barry said he expects Tuesday's vote to focus on the least controversial cuts—the hiring freeze and some administrative reductions—while punting decisions on libraries, roads, and beach services to subsequent meetings.

"Nobody wants to cut services," Barry said. "But we can't spend money we don't have."

Some commissioners have floated alternatives to cuts. Commissioner May suggested drawing from the county's reserve fund, which currently holds $24 million—roughly 8% of the general fund budget. Moreno cautioned against that approach, noting that county policy requires maintaining reserves of at least 6% and that credit rating agencies look unfavorably on reserve drawdowns.

Commissioner Doug Underhill, who represents District 2, proposed revisiting the county's tax increment financing agreements with the Community Redevelopment Agency, which diverts property tax growth in downtown Pensacola away from the county's general fund. That suggestion drew no support from other commissioners at Tuesday's workshop.

Public comment will be taken at the May 13 meeting. The commission chamber at 221 Palafox Place seats 150.

articles.label: Downtown
articles.headline: Three West Main Street buildings sit empty two years after incentive deals expired
articles.dek: City gave developers $1.8 million in tax breaks. Now the storefronts are dark and the owners aren't returning calls.
brief: Three renovated buildings on West Main Street have stood vacant since late 2024 despite receiving $1.8 million in city tax incentives
The incentive agreements required five years of commercial occupancy, but enforcement mechanisms remain unclear
City officials say they are reviewing options but have not initiated clawback proceedings
articles.body:
The coffee shop closed first. Then the gallery. By November 2024, all three storefronts at 118, 122, and 126 West Main Street had gone dark. Paper still covers the windows at the old Pressed & Bound café, edges curling in the humidity. A faded "Coming Soon" sign hangs crooked in the gallery space next door.

Two years later, nothing has come.

These buildings were supposed to anchor downtown's western corridor. In 2017 and 2018, the Pensacola City Council approved a combined $1.8 million in tax increment financing and façade improvement grants for their renovation. The developers—two LLCs registered to addresses in Birmingham and Atlanta—promised mixed-use spaces that would bring foot traffic west of Palafox.

The incentive agreements expired in 2024. The occupancy requirements that came with them appear to have been unmet. And the city has yet to take any action to recover the funds.

The deals

Tax increment financing, or TIF, allows cities to rebate a portion of increased property tax revenue back to developers who invest in designated redevelopment zones. Pensacola's Community Redevelopment Agency oversees downtown's TIF district.

According to documents obtained through a public records request, WMS Holdings LLC received $1.2 million in TIF rebates between 2018 and 2023 for renovations at 122 and 126 West Main. A separate entity, Mainline Development Group, received $600,000 in façade grants and TIF funds for 118 West Main.

Both agreements included occupancy clauses. The buildings were required to maintain commercial tenants for at least five years following the completion of renovations. If that requirement went unmet, the city could initiate proceedings to recover a prorated share of the incentives.

Renovations at all three addresses were completed by late 2019. The five-year clock started ticking.

What happened

For a while, the buildings delivered on their promise. Pressed & Bound opened in early 2020, serving coffee and hosting small concerts. A gallery called Liminal Space took the middle storefront. The third building housed a short-lived co-working space that closed during the pandemic and was replaced by a vintage furniture dealer.

By 2023, the furniture store had relocated to East Hill. Liminal Space followed in early 2024, its owner citing rising rent. Pressed & Bound held on until September 2024, when a handwritten note appeared on the door thanking customers for four years of support.

The buildings have been vacant since.

The Flightline attempted to contact representatives of both WMS Holdings and Mainline Development Group. Phone numbers listed in state corporate filings were disconnected. Emails to addresses on file with the Florida Division of Corporations went unanswered. A certified letter sent to the Birmingham address listed for WMS Holdings was returned as undeliverable.

Property records show all three buildings remain under the same LLC ownership. Property taxes are current.

City response

Pensacola CRA Director Marcus Webb confirmed in an email that his office is "aware of the vacancy status" at the West Main Street properties and is "reviewing the terms of the original agreements to determine appropriate next steps."

Asked whether the city had initiated clawback proceedings or made formal contact with the property owners, Webb declined to comment further, citing "ongoing review."

City Council member Allison Patton, whose district includes West Main Street, said she has received complaints from neighboring business owners about the vacant storefronts.

"People want to know what happened to all that money," Patton said. "I want to know too. These deals were made before I was on the council, but the accountability belongs to all of us now."

Patton said she plans to request a full accounting of CRA-funded projects and their compliance status at the June council meeting.

Questions remain

The incentive agreements, while public records, do not specify clear enforcement timelines. Clawback provisions exist but require the city to demonstrate noncompliance and initiate legal proceedings—a process that can take months or years and may ultimately cost more than it recovers.

Meanwhile, the buildings sit. Paint peels on the restored façades. The brass door handles at 126 West Main have begun to oxidize.

Three blocks east, Palafox Street bustles on weekend evenings. Tourists photograph the murals. Restaurants fill. The promised westward expansion of downtown energy has not materialized.

John Carruthers owns a print shop at the corner of West Main and DeVilliers. He has watched the empty storefronts for two years.

"They told us this was going to be the next big thing," Carruthers said. "I'm still waiting."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors and a test for beach traffic plan
articles.dek: New shuttle system from Pensacola Beach launches Friday. County says it learned from last year's gridlock. Residents aren't convinced.
brief: Escambia County launches new shuttle service from Pensacola Beach to NAS Pensacola for Blue Angels homecoming show May 15-16
Officials expect 200,000 total visitors across the weekend, with enhanced traffic management after 2025 gridlock stranded thousands
Beach residents express skepticism about shuttle capacity and timing, citing previous years' failures
articles.body:
The parking lot at Casino Beach sat empty at 7 a.m. Thursday morning. By this time next week, every space will be gone before sunrise.

Blue Angels homecoming weekend arrives May 15-16, and Escambia County officials say they're ready this time. A new shuttle system will run continuous loops from Pensacola Beach to NAS Pensacola's back gate, part of a traffic management plan the county hopes will prevent a repeat of last year's mess.

"We heard the community loud and clear," said Escambia County Public Safety Director Eric Gilmore at a press briefing Wednesday. "The 2025 show created unacceptable conditions. We've rebuilt this plan from the ground up."

Last year's homecoming stranded thousands of beachgoers in gridlock on the Bob Sikes Bridge for up to four hours. Emergency vehicles couldn't reach Pensacola Beach for most of Saturday afternoon. The county faced a flood of complaints and a formal review from the Board of County Commissioners.

The new plan

This year's approach centers on three changes: earlier road closures, expanded shuttle service, and real-time traffic monitoring through a new app partnership with the Florida Department of Transportation.

Via Pensacola Beach will close to inbound traffic at 8 a.m. both days instead of 10 a.m. Shuttles will depart from the Pensacola Beach Boardwalk parking structure every 10 minutes starting at 7 a.m., with a dedicated lane on Gulf Breeze Parkway for the 40-minute trip to NAS Pensacola's Barrancas gate.

The county contracted with Escambia County Area Transit and two private charter companies to provide 25 buses. Gilmore said the system can move 3,000 passengers per hour at full capacity.

"That's a significant improvement over personal vehicle traffic through the main gates," Gilmore said. "We're asking people to trust the system."

Residents aren't buying it

Trust is in short supply on Pensacola Beach.

Portofino Tower resident Jim Kendall has lived on the beach for 11 years. He's watched every homecoming show from his balcony. He's also watched every traffic disaster.

"They say this every year," Kendall said Thursday, standing outside the Portofino lobby. "New plan. Lessons learned. Then Saturday comes and my wife can't get to the grocery store for six hours."

Kendall pointed to the shuttle's 7 a.m. start time. Practice shows begin at 11 a.m. Most spectators want to arrive by 9 a.m. to claim viewing spots.

"You're telling me 25 buses are going to move everyone who wants to be there by nine?" he said. "Do the math."

The math: If 50,000 people want to reach NAS Pensacola from the beach by 9 a.m., the shuttle system would need to complete roughly 17 full cycles in two hours. At 10-minute intervals, that's six cycles maximum. Even with the county's projected 3,000-per-hour capacity, the system could move 6,000 people in that window.

County officials acknowledge the shuttle won't handle all beach traffic. They're encouraging visitors staying on Pensacola Beach to use the Quietwater Beach viewing area instead of traveling to NAS Pensacola.

"The beach offers excellent sight lines for the demonstration," Gilmore said. "Not everyone needs to be on station."

200,000 expected

Visit Pensacola projects 200,000 total visitors across the homecoming weekend, matching last year's attendance. Hotel occupancy on Pensacola Beach hit 98% for Saturday night within hours of bookings opening in January.

The economic impact estimate: $35 million in direct visitor spending, according to Visit Pensacola President Darien Schaefer.

"This is our Super Bowl," Schaefer said. "The Blue Angels are synonymous with Pensacola. People travel from across the country for this weekend."

NAS Pensacola's main gates will open at 8 a.m. both days. The base expects 40,000 spectators on the flight line Saturday and 35,000 Sunday. Gates close when parking reaches capacity, typically by 10 a.m. on Saturday.

The Blue Angels will perform their full demonstration both days, weather permitting. Friday's practice show—open to the public from Quietwater Beach and other off-base viewing areas—begins at 11 a.m.

What residents want

The Pensacola Beach Advocates, a resident group, submitted a list of requests to the county commission in March. They asked for guaranteed emergency vehicle access, a resident-only lane on the Bob Sikes Bridge, and a cap on daily visitors.

The county denied the resident lane as legally unworkable on a public road. The visitor cap was deemed unenforceable. Emergency access, Gilmore said, will be maintained through coordination with the Pensacola Beach Fire Department and Escambia County EMS.

"We will have units pre-positioned on the beach throughout the weekend," Gilmore said. "If the bridge locks up, those units are already in place."

Advocates president Marcy Littleton called that response inadequate.

"Pre-positioned units help with what's already on the beach," Littleton said Thursday. "What about cardiac calls that need a hospital? What about structure fires that need backup?"

The county's plan includes helicopter evacuation protocols for medical emergencies that cannot wait for ground transport. Gilmore declined to specify response time guarantees.

A waiting game

Thursday afternoon, workers installed temporary barriers along Via Pensacola Beach near the toll plaza. Electronic signs flashed shuttle information. A county drone crew tested equipment that will monitor traffic flow in real time.

The preparation is visible. Whether it's sufficient won't be clear until Saturday morning, when the first wave of visitors hits the Bob Sikes Bridge and the plan meets reality.

Kendall said he's already stocked his refrigerator for the weekend. He doesn't plan to leave the island.

"I'll watch the show from my balcony," he said. "Same as always. And I'll watch the traffic from there too. That's usually the more interesting show."

The Blue Angels homecoming show runs Saturday and Sunday, May 15-16, with gates opening at 8 a.m. at NAS Pensacola. Friday's practice show is viewable from Quietwater Beach and other public areas. Shuttles from Pensacola Beach begin at 7 a.m. Saturday and Sunday. Real-time traffic updates will be available through the FL511 app.
